summary: Defines how to carry Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST) messages over secure CoAP instead of HTTPS. EST is a way for devices to get certificates, and CoAP is a lightweight protocol common on small, low-power devices. This lets constrained devices reuse existing EST functionality to obtain certificates.

plainLanguage.summary: A tiny device wants an ID card from the office. Instead of the long form, it uses a short, light version of the same request.

questions: how do iot devices get certificates
how do iot devices get certificates over coap
subtitle: How small, low-power devices get their certificates by running EST over secure CoAP instead of HTTPS.

tldr.problem: EST hands out certificates over HTTPS, but many Internet of Things devices speak the lightweight CoAP protocol instead of HTTP and cannot afford the full web stack.
tldr.mechanism: EST-coaps carries the same EST messages over CoAP secured with DTLS. It shortens the URLs, sends binary payloads instead of Base64, and uses CoAP block-wise transfer to split large messages.
tldr.outcome: Constrained devices can enroll for certificates with existing EST functionality. RFC 9148 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9908.

facts.label: Binary payload saving
facts.value: 30% smaller than Base64 for DER-encoded ASN.1

today: RFC 9148 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9908. It has not been obsoleted, so it remains the specification of EST over secure CoAP.

sections.title: EST for Constrained Devices
sections.content:
Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST, RFC 7030) lets an endpoint get a certificate, and optionally a key, from a Certification Authority (CA) or Registration Authority (RA). EST carries its messages over HTTPS.

Some Internet of Things devices use the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) instead of HTTP. RFC 9148 defines a new transport for EST that uses DTLS and CoAP in place of TLS and HTTP. EST responses can be large, so it also uses CoAP Block-Wise Transfer (RFC 7959) to fragment messages at the CoAP layer.

The document profiles EST for certificate-based client authentication only. HTTP Basic and Digest authentication are not supported, and the client MUST be authenticated for all functions, even those that RFC 7030 allows without authentication.

Much of the text is directly traceable to RFC 7030. The EST-coaps design follows the EST design closely.
sections.plainLanguage: Big computers get their ID cards through a busy front desk. Tiny devices cannot handle that crowd, so this gives them a quiet side door that does the same job.

sections.title: DTLS Security and Authentication
sections.content:
EST-coaps relies on a secure transport for CoAP, and DTLS is the one it uses. In line with the IoT profiles in RFC 7925, the mandatory cipher suite is TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8, and the curve secp256r1 MUST be supported. The text notes that support for Curve25519 will likely be required in future IoT profiles.

The client authenticates the server with certificates in the DTLS handshake. The client MUST be configured with at least an Implicit Trust Anchor database so that it can check the server the first time, before it updates its trust anchors. The server authenticates the client with a client certificate. That can be a previously issued certificate, which is common for simple re-enrollment, or a previously installed one such as a manufacturer IDevID. If an IDevID has expired, the server MAY still accept it.

Proof that the client holds the private key (proof-of-possession) is OPTIONAL. When it is wanted, the client puts channel-binding information into the challengePassword attribute of its PKCS #10 request: the DTLS Finished message (tls-unique) for DTLS 1.2, or a 32-byte tls-exporter value for DTLS 1.3.

Unlike plain EST, an EST-coaps DTLS connection MAY stay open for several EST transactions in a row, for example a /crts request followed by a /sen request. It SHOULD only be kept alive for requests close together. For devices that sleep, connection IDs (RFC 9146) or DTLS session resumption can avoid a full new handshake.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the office hands over an ID card, the device and the office show each other proof of who they are, like two people checking each other's badges at a locked door.

sections.title: Short URIs and Discovery
sections.content:
Packets on low-resource networks are small, so EST-coaps shortens the EST paths. Resources live under /.well-known/est/, optionally followed by an arbitrary label that a CA can use to pick a certificate profile, then a short name. Clients and servers MUST support the short URIs.

Not every EST function is required. /cacerts, /simpleenroll and /simplereenroll are mandatory to implement. /serverkeygen and /csrattrs are optional. /fullcmc is not specified because it was judged too expensive for low-resource devices.

A client that does not know what a server offers sends a GET to /.well-known/core with the resource type ace.est*. The server MUST support the default /.well-known/est root resource and SHOULD support discovery when it uses other paths or ports. The first three resources (crts, sen, sren) MUST be listed in a discovery response; the others appear only if implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: The long street address is shortened to a nickname so it fits on a tiny label. If you do not know what the office offers, you can ask it for a menu first.

sections.title: Payload Formats and Response Codes
sections.content:
EST sends Base64 text. EST-coaps does not need to: the payload follows the ASN.1 structure of the media type and is sent as plain binary, which the RFC says is 30% smaller for DER-encoded ASN.1. The CoAP Content-Format option (the HTTP Content-Type equivalent) says which EST message is inside. Format 281 carries certificates in a PKCS #7 container and MUST be supported by servers; 287 carries a single certificate; 286 is used for enrollment requests and 285 for CSR attribute responses.

Server-side key generation answers use Content-Format 62 (application/multipart-core), a CBOR array that pairs each part with its own Content-Format identifier, so the private key and the certificate can come in either order.

Response codes map from HTTP to CoAP: 2.05 is success for GET requests (/crts, /att), 2.04 is success for POST requests, and 4.04 means the resource is not available. HTTP 400, 401, 403, 404 and 503 map to 4.00, 4.01, 4.03, 4.04 and 5.03. Requests are RECOMMENDED to be sent as Confirmable CoAP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing a message in a long coded alphabet, the device just sends the raw bytes, which makes the message much shorter. A little tag on the front says what kind of message it is.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Delayed Responses
sections.content:
Certificates can be bigger than one small packet. For 256-bit curves, ECDSA certificates are commonly 500 to 1000 bytes, and 384-bit ones can reach 1.5KB. A /cacerts response may hold several. CoAP suggests upper bounds of 1152 bytes for a message and 1024 bytes for its payload when nothing is known about the headers, so EST-coaps must split messages.

It uses the Block1 option for request payloads and Block2 for responses. Servers MUST implement both. Clients MUST implement Block2, and Block1 only if they send requests larger than the path MTU. Size1 and Size2 are optional.

A server may need time to produce a certificate. A moderately slow server sends an empty ACK (0.00) and later returns the certificate as 2.04. A very slow server (the RFC mentions manual intervention taking minutes) SHOULD answer with 5.03 and a Max-Age option. The client SHOULD wait that long and then resend the identical CSR, repeating until it gets the certificate or gives up.
sections.plainLanguage: If a parcel is too big for the mail slot, you send it in pieces. If the office needs time to make your card, it tells you to come back in a while and ask again.

sections.title: Server-Side Key Generation
sections.content:
A client can ask the server to generate its private key as well as the certificate. The RFC lists reasons: it may be more secure to generate the key centrally, key generation may be expensive for the device, or policy may require central control. The server treats the CSR like any other, except that it MUST ignore the public key and signature in it.

A /skg request asks for a PKCS #7 certificate plus the key. A /skc request asks for a single application/pkix-cert certificate plus the key. Either way, a private key MUST be returned.

The key comes back either unprotected as PKCS #8 (Content-Format 284) or inside CMS (Content-Format 280), when the CSR carries SMIMECapabilities and a decrypt key identifier. Implementations that support server-side key generation MUST support unprotected keys. Encrypting the key SHOULD be supported where end-to-end encryption is needed between client and server, for example when a Registrar sits in between.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the office makes the secret key for you, because that is easier for a tiny device. It can lock the key in a box that only you can open.

sections.title: The EST-coaps-to-HTTPS Registrar
sections.content:
The EST server may live outside the constrained network and speak TLS and HTTP. A Registrar at the edge then terminates EST-coaps on the device side and opens EST over TLS to the server on the other side. It MUST authenticate the client, may authorize it, and MUST itself be authenticated by the EST server or CA.

The Registrar translates URIs using the short-path table, maps CoAP codes to HTTP status codes, and converts between CBOR byte strings and Base64. It MUST reassemble blocks before translating a message and MUST support resource discovery. The CMS-encrypted private key is converted without being decrypted.

There is a cost. Proof-of-possession linking cannot be enforced end to end, because the Registrar sets up a new TLS connection upstream. The EST server learns it is talking to a Registrar from the id-kp-cmcRA extended key usage in its certificate. The RFC also says it is up to network designers which devices run EST at all, since some classes of constrained devices will not have enough resources for the payloads.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper stands at the edge of the little network. It speaks the device's short language on one side and the office's long language on the other, and passes messages back and forth.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most of the security considerations of RFC 7030 still apply, except those about passwords, since HTTP Basic authentication is not supported. The RFC stresses good random numbers: many constrained devices lack the entropy sources of a PC, so suitable hardware matters. Moving a private key from server to device is described as inherently risky, and anyone deploying server-side key generation SHOULD analyze whether it raises or lowers the risk of identity theft.

The Implicit Trust Anchor database should be carefully managed, and disabled after the CA certificates are received, which limits exposure to the first exchange. A client that sends other requests on the same DTLS connection after a /crts SHOULD revalidate the server chain against the updated Explicit trust anchors.

Cipher suites with _EXPORT_ or _DES_ in the name MUST NOT be used. For DTLS 1.2, tls-unique is still used even though the 3SHAKE attack is a known risk, because that attack does not expose EST-coaps messages. Implementers should use the Extended Master Secret extension, and DTLS 1.3 uses tls-exporter instead. With a Registrar and no end-to-end encryption, the Registrar may see a server-generated private key, so the client must trust it.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the list of people you trust short and well checked, make your secret numbers truly random, and remember that a helper in the middle could peek at a secret key unless it is locked in a box.
